intro: Every day the dice roll a premise and a dozen constraints, and the game has to honour all of them. Tonight's roll was seed 288762830: a trumpet who is secretly royalty, composting socks, out of duty. Here is how that became a palace kitchen garden, an attic full of socks and a very strict man called Ormsby.

rolls.value: a trumpet who is secretly royalty
rolls.became: In 1791 King Humphrey the Tidy left his kingdom to “my trumpet, which never once let me down.” Nobody checked the paperwork. So the trumpet in the kitchen garden is, legally, the monarch. It doesn't know. The audio guide does, and keeps quiet.

Rule One of the household (1702) says nothing of the Crown may ever leave the palace, so nothing can be thrown away. Compost is the loophole: a sock that becomes soil in the palace garden has never left the palace. Mr Ormsby, who checks these things, has checked.

Two centuries of royal socks, kept under Rule One, fill the attic to the rafters: the Monday Sock, the Toe Sock (a scandal in 1840), the Sock with a Message, the gold Coronation Sock. Wool really does compost.

Ormsby empties the attic out of its windows into the garden (still the palace). A trumpet's bell is a funnel, so the trumpet catches them. The ones you miss land among the tourists, and one of them pockets a souvenir. That's a breach of Rule One.
Everything stays small enough to count on a blackboard: soil in the tens, a heap that holds a few dozen socks, forty trunks, twelve kinds of sock.
Nobody asked the trumpet to do this. It's the household's trumpet, the attic is falling in, and the tour is getting socks on its head. So it does its duty, one sock at a time.

Rule One, and the man who keeps it: Ormsby only drops a sock when the heap has room for it, opens no trunk past the sixteenth until the Household Book is done, and has a list of every souvenir, in alphabetical order, by sock.
Mr Ormsby, Keeper of the Household Rules.
About an hour and a half: forty trunks, the Book, Rule Two and the King's trunk. The heap keeps rotting while you're away, and the upside-down brollies keep catching, at a gentle pace.
The Household Book: every kind of royal sock must be catalogued, one of each, caught as Ormsby finds them in deeper and deeper trunks. Each one gets its own stop on the audio guide.

rolls.value: a mid-game rule change that reshapes everything
rolls.became: Handing in the finished Book makes Ormsby read the back page: Rule Two (1702), “What the Crown has paired, let no one part.” From then on only pairs go in the heap. Odd socks wait on a washing line for their partner, so you stop catching everything and start catching the right ones.

rolls.value: storage caps you must build past
rolls.became: The heap only holds so much and Ormsby won't drop a sock without room for it, so you build bins. After Rule Two the washing line only holds so many odd socks, so you buy pegs.
When forty trunks are empty, Ormsby unlocks the last one, King Humphrey's own, and tips the lot out of every window at once: a pair of every kind, and whatever you miss is thrown back up.

After the last pair, the King's will flutters down too. The trumpet catches it, doesn't read it, and composts it with everything else. It never becomes King. It gets something smaller: its own stop on the audio guide, Stop 14a, which was blank the whole game.
The whole garden is drawn in chalk on the potting-shed blackboard, in a wooden frame, with the rubbed-out ghosts of earlier lessons.
A teal-green board and a box of coloured chalk: brass for the trumpet, primrose for the important bits, and every sock in its own stick.

A dusty, laid-back beat in G mixolydian (the F natural is the colour) with warm electric piano, a round bass and a muted trumpet, the main character, on the tune. Rule Two, the King's trunk and the ending each reshape it. The catches climb the same scale.
Every line is the palace's audio guide: numbered stops, “please note the trumpet in the portrait,” and a polite refusal to draw conclusions. The tourists on the path are listening to it too.
No calendar nod today. Just socks.

outro: In short: a strict rule made an attic of socks, a trumpet's bell made a catcher, compost made a loophole, and a king's will made a footnote. Please do not lean on the heap.
